IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States
————
   N O. 25-417
FRANCIS NIELSEN,
   Petitioner,
v.
KEKAI WATANABE,
     R e s p o n d e n t .
————
On Writ of Certiorari
 to the United States Court of Appeals
for the Ninth Circuit
————
REPLY BRIEF FOR PETITIONER
————
Watanabe fails to show th at this case—or any case—
justifies the “ ‘disfavored judicial activity’ ” of “recognizing
a cause of action under Bivens.”  Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S.
482, 491 (2022).  Conceding that Bivens, Davis, and Carlson cannot be extended to any new context, Watanabe
admits he must lose if this context is new—if there is any
meaningful difference between this case and Carlson.
Resp.Br.1.  Such differences abound.  In Carlson, the
inmate died and there was no  opportunity to pursue
administrative or injunctive relief, making it “damages or
nothing.”  Here, Watanabe al leges a non-life-threatening
injury.  He could and did pursue non-damages relief.  And
Carlson did not consider a host of special factors—includ-

2

ing the Administrative Remedy Program, Prison Litigation Reform Act, PATRIOT Act, and Federal Prison
Oversight Act—that militate against a judicially created
damages remedy.  Because Congress  could think those
differences are meaningful when weighing the costs and
benefits of a damages remedy, only Congress can decide
whether to provide that remedy; courts may not.
Watanabe’s insistence that this case reflects “precisely”
the same context as Carlson, Resp.Br.2, is thus untenable.
He theorizes that Congress endorsed claims like his in the
PLRA or Westfall Act.  This Court has held the opposite:
The PLRA indicates “Congress does not want a damages
remedy,” while the Westfall Act “simply left Bivens where
it found it”—in the courts’ hands.  Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582
U.S. 120, 148 (2017); Hernández v. Mesa, 589 U.S. 93, 111
n.9 (2020).  Neither counsels Bivens’s retention, much less
its extension here.
Ultimately, Watanabe’s brief confirms that Bivens has
earned its retirement.  Watanabe admits that separation
of powers forecloses extending Bivens, Davis, and Carlson.  Resp.Br.4.  Yet he tries to lock in their encroachments on legislative power, as king the Court to declare,
“This far and no further.”  Re sp.Br.1.  That declaration
would doom this case, which seeks to push Carlson
“further.”  But it elides a deeper problem: Lower courts
cannot agree on where “this far ” ends and “further”
begins, as rampant conflicts in the circuits and 13 prior
cases in this Court make clear.  This Court could continue
trying to demarcate a “this-far-but-no-further” boundary,
as it has for the past 45 years.  Or it could lay Bivens and
its progeny to rest, stop offering plaintiffs false hope, and
return responsibility for legislating causes of action to Congress where it belongs.  Either way, reversal is warranted.

3

I. THE NINTH CIRCUIT IMPROPERLY EXTENDED BIVENS
TO A NEW CONTEXT
Watanabe concedes Bivens and Carlson cannot be
extended to “any new context. ”  Resp.Br.1.  But his contention that this case presents “precisely” the same context as Carlson , Resp.Br.2, overlooks basic principles.
This Court’s “understanding of a ‘new context’ is broad.”
Hernández, 589 U.S. at 102.  Even “small” differences can
be “meaningful” and thus present “a new Bivens context.”
Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 149.  The “new-context inquiry” is
“easily satisfied.”  Ibid.  Watanabe mentions none of that.
More fundamentally, Watanabe fails to appreciate that
the new-context inquiry requires a legislative perspective.
Pet.Br.22-24.  He urges it “is not a legislative task to determine whether a case presents a ‘meaningful’ difference
from a prior one.”  Resp.Br.46.  But recognizing a Bivens
remedy is a quintessentially “ legislative endeavor.”  Egbert, 596 U.S. at 491 (emphasis added).  Courts weighing
Bivens remedies must consider th e full “ ‘range of policy
considerations * * * a legisl ature would consider.’ ”  Ibid.
They must be mindful that “Congress is ‘far more competent than the Judiciary’ to weigh such policy considerations”; that “the Judiciary’s authority to do so at all is, at
best, uncertain”; and that, ultimately, the “only” question
is “whether there is any rational reason (even one) to think
that Congress is better suited to ‘weigh the costs and
benefits of allowing a damages action.’ ”  Id. at 491, 496.
Consequently, a new Bivens context arises whenever a
case presents any difference from Bivens, Davis, and
Carlson that Congress could think meaningful as a matter
of legislative policy.  If a difference could affect Congress’s view of a damages remedy’s costs and benefits,
Congress must make the choice—and courts must refrain
from recognizing such a remedy themselves.  Treating the

4

inquiry like an “ordinary judi cial exercise,” Resp.Br.46,
fails to afford “utmost deference to Congress’ preeminent
authority in this area,” Egbert, 596 U.S. at 492.
This case differs profoundly from Carlson in immediacy
and severity; risk of disruption to prison administration;
and alternative remedial stru ctures neither considered
nor available in Carlson.  Congress could find each of those
differences meaningful.
A. Differences in Nature, Severity, and Immediacy
Make This a New Context from Carlson
1. Watanabe nowhere denies that in Carlson—as in
Bivens and Davis—it was “damages or nothing.”  Pet.Br.25.
The rapidly unfolding emergency, and the inmate’s
resulting death, left no opportunity to seek administrative
or injunctive relief.  Not so  here: Watanabe concedes he
could and did pursue administrative and injunctive relief
for the treatment he seeks.  Resp.Br.23.  That makes this
a new context.  “Damages or nothing” is foundational to
Bivens.  Pet.Br.25-27.  Congre ss could readily find cases
that are not “damages or nothing” meaningfully different.
Watanabe insists “damages or nothing” should be irrelevant to Carlson claims.  Resp.Br.21.  Congress could think
otherwise.  This Court has held otherwise: Ziglar (cited
Resp.Br.21-22) held the plaintiffs sought “to extend Carlson to a new context” because “an injunction” or other nondamages relief might be available.  582 U.S. at 147-148.
Watanabe’s contention that the PLRA “endorsed” Bivens damages where other relief is available, Resp.Br.22,
lacks merit.  The PLRA’s failure to provide a “standalone
damages remedy against federal jailers” indicates “Congress does not want a damages remedy.”  Ziglar, 582 U.S.
at 148-149 (emphasis added); see pp. 10-11, 21-22, infra.  It
certainly does not support creating Bivens remedies where

5

Bivens’s own logic doesn’t.  No r does the principle that
injunctions are “available only where there is no adequate
remedy at law,” Resp.Br. 22, license courts to invent
damages remedies where “traditional equitable powers
suffice,” Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 133.
Watanabe’s case is not “ ‘damages or nothing.’ ”
Resp.Br.21, 23-24.  Watanabe admits he could—and did—
seek prospective relief through the ARP and in court.
Resp.Br.23.  Even if prospective relief would not remedy
past harm, Resp.Br.21, it does not “matter that ‘existing
remedies do not provide complete relief,’ ” Egbert, 596
U.S. at 493.  Ziglar held the possibility of “an injunction”
presented “a new context” from Carlson even though the
plaintiffs also alleged past pain and suffering.  582 U.S. at
128, 147-148.
Watanabe’s release from pr ison, Resp.Br.23, does not
alter the result.  Even if prospective relief ( e.g., ordering
the government to provide unconstitutionally denied treatment) were no longer possible—a proposition Watanabe
does not try to prove—Watanabe still had years to pursue
non-monetary relief.  The inmate in Carlson  had no such
opportunity.  Congre ss could easily think that difference
meaningful.
2. Congress could also find that, even if  personal damages liability were appropriate in extreme cases like
Carlson where death results, cases involving less severe
injuries present a different policy balance.  Pet.Br.27-31.
Watanabe does not deny that Congress regularly draws
such lines, singling out conduct resulting in death.
Pet.Br.27-28 & n.10.  He obje cts that “most of those statutes only enhance the remedy available if death ensues.”
Resp.Br.20.  But Watanabe admits Congress has created
a “[c]ause of ac tion” available only in cases of “death.”

6

46 U.S.C. § 30302 (cited Resp.Br.20).  And he misses the
point.  Bivens is “ ‘solely’ ” about imposing enhanced “ ‘deterr[ence]’ ” beyond other deterrents like agency discipline.
Egbert, 596 U.S. at 498.  The cited statutes show Congress
regularly finds differences in severity, including death and
life-threatening injury, meaningful when setting appropriate deterrence.  Here, too, Congress could conclude that enhanced deterrence should be re served for cases involving
death.  Whatever line Congress might draw, “calibrat[ing]”
“deterrence” is a “legislative  d e t e r m i n a t i o n  t h a t  m u s t  b e
left to Congress, not the federal courts.”  Ibid.
Congress could draw from this Court’s repeated observation that “death is different” because of its “severity.”
Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U.S. 153, 187-188 (1976) (plurality
opinion).  While death does not per se violate the Eighth
Amendment, Resp.Br.20-21, there is a long history of imposing protections unique to cases involving death—and,
more importantly, Congress could do so as a matter of
policy.  Pet.Br.27-28.  Despite Watanabe’s protestation,
Resp.Br.21, that is so even if the death involves a “sudden
killing” rather than “prolonged physical and mental suffering,” Kennedy v. Louisiana, 554 U.S. 407, 435 (2008).
The “qualitative difference between death and all other”
consequences, Harmelin v. Michigan, 501 U.S. 957, 995
(1991), makes this context new.
So does the “risk of disrupti ve intrusion by the Judiciary into the functioning of other branches.”  Ziglar, 582
U.S. at 140; Pet.Br.28-29.  Watanabe asserts that cases
like his involve “the same (or less) risk of disruptive intrusion” as Carlson .  Resp.Br.15.  But Congress could find
any disruption risk tolerable only in extreme cases like
Carlson.  And Watanabe has no answer to the heightened
disruptions Nielsen identified.  Pet.Br.29.  Suits based on
less severe incidents are far more likely to be used to

7

harass prison staff than suits based on inmate deaths.
They are vastly more common, threatening more disruption and financial impact.  And fear of liability can spur
costly defensive medicine—such as acquiescing to demands for hospital transfers regardless of medical necessity.  Each of those “negative systemic consequences” could
affect Congress’s view of the relative costs and benefits of
a Bivens remedy.  Goldey v. Fields, 606 U.S. 942, 944
(2025) (per curiam).  Watanabe addresses none of them.
This case illustrates those stakes.  Watanabe complains
he was not sent to a hospital  or specialist for months
despite multiple requests to  prison administrators.
Resp.Br.10.  But he alleges on ly a single encounter with
Nielsen, a line-level paramedic who (in consultation with
an on-call physician) provided medication and advised
follow-up treatment shortly af ter Watanabe was injured,
while declining to send him to  the hospital.  Pet.Br.12-13
& n.8.  For that one event, Watanabe seeks to hold Nielsen
personally liable for $3 million.  As Watanabe’s own amici
recognize, delays in specialized treatment often result
from “institutional,” “system-wide constraints,” including
staffing shortages and challenges with secure transportation.  Med.Justice.Br.4, 9-13.   Congress could conclude
that allowing Bivens suits in such cases unacceptably
exposes prison staff to indi vidual liability for—and may
interfere with—fundamentally institutional decisions.
Congress could readily distinguish such cases from Carlson, where an emergency presen ted prison staff with a
straightforward duty to try to save the inmate’s life.
Nor does Carlson itself foreclose distinguishing between
life and death.  Resp.Br.18-19.  Carlson’s first sentence
describes the case as invo lving “personal injuries from
which [the inmate] died ,” and its “survivorship” holding
simply states that death will not bar a “ ‘Bivens-type action

8

brought against defendants whose conduct results in
death.’ ”  Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14, 16, 23-24 (1980) (emphasis added).  Watanabe invokes a supposed “first holding
that the decedent had a cause of  action before his death.”
Resp.Br.18.  There is no such holding.  The first question
presented was whether the FTCA barred a Bivens remedy.
446 U.S. at 16-17.  And the Court declined to decide whether
the complaint asserted only “the decedent’s own claim”
(Resp.Br.18) or also his mother ’s “wrongful-death” claim.
446 U.S. at 17-18 n.4.  “Resolut ion” of that question was
“irrelevant” given the Court’s view that Bivens’s “deterrence goals” favored a damages remedy where “ ‘conduct
results in death.’ ”  Id. at 18 n.4, 24-25.  Carlson may have
assumed the inmate would have had a claim had he lived.
But assumptions are not holding s.  They certainly do not
foreclose Congress’s recognizing a meaningful difference
between life and death.
B. Special Factors Not Considered in Carlson Make
the Context New
This case also implicates “s pecial factors that previous
Bivens cases did not consider”—including “alternative remedial structure[s]” and post-Carlson “legislative action.”
Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 137, 139-140 , 148-149.  That, too,
renders this Bivens context “new.”  Pet.Br.32-39.
1. Watanabe cannot deny that this Court has identified the ARP’s “ ‘alternative remedial structure’ ” as a
“ ‘special facto[r].’ ”  Goldey, 606 U.S. at 944.  Nor does he
deny the ARP was “not considered” in Carlson.  Ziglar,
582 U.S. at 148.  That makes the context “new.”  Ibid.
Invoking Carlson’s conclusion that the Federal Tort
Claims Act was an inadequate remedy, Watanabe urges
the Court to apply the “sam e analysis” to the ARP.
Resp.Br.25; see Pet.Br.38-39.  But Bivens plaintiffs must
satisfy the current “prevailing framework,” including its

9

treatment of “ ‘remedial mechanisms’ ” and “ ‘special factors.’ ”  Egbert, 596 U.S. at 501.  Under that framework, it
is irrelevant whether alternative remedies are “ ‘equally
effective,’ ” ibid. (quoting Carlson , 446 U.S. at 19)—as
Watanabe elsewhere concedes, Resp.Br.25.  Nor did Carlson’s FTCA analysis “necessarily subsum[e] the lesser
remedy of the ARP.”  Resp. B r . 2 6 .   T h e  A R P  i s  n o t  a
“lesser” remedy—it is a different remedy.  The FTCA
allows only damages, while the ARP offers specific relief,
such as medical care.  Carlson said nothing about the
latter remedy, which may offer “a faster and more direct
route to relief than a suit for money damages.”  Ziglar, 582
U.S. at 145.  Under the prevailing Bivens framework, the
ARP makes the context new.
That the ARP “existed” at the time of Carlson, Resp.Br.24-
25, is irrelevant.  Pet.Br.37-38.  What matters is that it was
“not considered.”  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148 (emphasis added).  Watanabe does not dispute, moreover, that neither the
inmate nor the plaintiff in Carlson could have used the
ARP.  Pet.Br.38; Pet.App.98a.  Watanabe says only the
remedy’s “existence ” matters, not its  “effectiveness or
availability to any particular plaintiff.”  Resp.Br.25.  That’s
true enough when a remedy is considered.  But it does not
defeat finding a new context based on a remedy that was
neither available nor considered in prior cases.  Ziglar, for
example, found the context “new” based on the possibility
of injunctive relief.  582 U.S. at 148.  Injunctions existed at
the time of Carlson.  Ziglar found they created a “new
context” anyway, because they  were “not considered” or
“available” in Carlson.  Ibid.  Same with the ARP (and injunctive relief) here.  Pet.Br.38.  Watanabe has no response.1

1 Watanabe gets nowhere by invoki ng an uncodified ARP precursor
that “existed” when the inmate in Carlson died.  Resp.Br.24-25.  That
precursor also was not available, and certainly “not considered,” in

10

2. Post- Carlson legislation—the PLRA, PATRIOT
Act, and Federal Prison Oversight Act—also renders the
context new.  Pet.Br.33-35, 38.  Each statute addresses
prisoner complaints, yet none provides a damages remedy.  They are “legislative action suggesting that Congress
does not want a damages reme dy”—“a factor counseling
hesitation” that both presents a new context and forecloses Bivens’s extension.  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148-149; see
Goldey, 606 U.S. at 944.
Watanabe says the PLRA supports him because it does
not expressly “eliminate Carlson claims.”  Resp.Br.27.
But this Court has already held that, as post-Carlson legislation addressing prisoner suits, the PLRA renders the
context “new.”  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148.  Watanabe’s argument isn’t really that the PLRA doesn’t make the context
new; it is, at most, an argu ment that the difference in
context does not counsel against extending Carlson to this
new context at Bivens step two.  But Watanabe has conceded his claim cannot survive at step two.  Pet.Br.39.  And
this Court has held that the PLRA forecloses Bivens’s
extension at step two.  Goldey, 606 U.S. at 944.
Watanabe overreads the PLRA regardless.  Despite
Watanabe’s effort to portray it as Carlson-specific legislation, Resp.Br.27, th e PLRA applies to all prisoner suits,
including suits authorized by statute (e.g., 42 U.S.C. § 1983
or the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, § 2000bb-1(c))
or seeking injunctive relief.  § 1997e(a).  Requiring that all
prisoners exhaust administrative remedies does not
suggest Congress endorsed a judicially created damages
claim—especially where the existence of “alternative

Carlson.  It is also waived: Watanabe’s  brief in opposition conceded
“the ARP was not in place when the inmate in Carlson died.”
Br.in.Opp.15; see this Court’s Rule 15.2.

11

remedial structures” itself “foreclose[s]” a claim.  Egbert,
596 U.S. at 493, 497; see Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148-149 (discussing PLRA).  Nor does  the PLRA’s blanket bar  on
emotional and mental damage s absent physical injury,
§ 1997e(e); Resp.Br.20, suggest  a damages remedy is
available whenever physical injury occurs, see Goldey, 606
U.S. at 943-944.
Watanabe invokes McCarthy v. Madigan, 503 U.S. 140
(1992), Resp.Br.16, 22-23, 26- 27, but does not argue it
requires recognizing a Bivens remedy despite the ARP.
McCarthy concerned exhaustion, not the propriety of a
Bivens remedy.  Cf. Egbert, 596 U.S. at 498 (explaining
that articulation of requir ements for First Amendment
Bivens claim in Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.S. 250 (2006),
was not a holding that Bivens allows First Amendment
claims).  In holding that Bivens plaintiffs need not pursue
ARP remedies, moreover, McCarthy emphasized that
doing so was not “mandated by  Congress.”  503 U.S. at
149.  After the PLRA, it is.
Nor was McCarthy (or Congress’s response) peculiar
to Bivens claims.  McCarthy reasoned by analogy to
then-current § 1997e(a), which applied only to state prisoners and was largely discretionary.  Booth v. Churner, 532
U.S. 731, 739-740 (2 001) (discussing McCarthy) .   I n  t h e
PLRA, “Congress replaced th e text of the statute as
construed in McCarthy” to mandate exhaustion for both
state and federal prisoners, regardless of relief sought.  Id.
at 740.  Thus, while the PLRA’s exhaustion requirement
would reach Bivens claims (as this Court has observed “in
dicta,” Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 149), it is a global requirement
that applies equally to prisoners suing under § 1983 or
RFRA.  And, as discussed,  the PLRA nowhere purports
to authorize Bivens claims at all, much less ones foreclosed
by this Court’s current Bivens doctrine.

12

3. Watanabe barely addresses PATRIOT Act § 1001
and the Federal Prison Oversight Act.  He nowhere denies
their “investigation” and “grievance process[es]” closely
resemble those that foreclosed a Bivens remedy in Egbert.
596 U.S. at 497-498; see Pet.Br. 34-35.  His assertion that
PATRIOT Act § 1001 does not “concer[n] prisoner claims
for deliberate indifference to a serious medical condition,”
Resp.Br.28, is incorrect.  It broadly covers alleged “abuses
of civil rights” by Justice Department employees, including Bureau of Prisons staff.  115 Stat. 391, § 1001(1).
Regardless, the Oversight Act expressly addresses
prisoner medical complaints.  Pet.Br.34-35.  That it “was
not in place when [Watanabe was injured] is immaterial”
by Watanabe’s own admission: “The Bivens inquiry does
not turn on whether an alternative remedy was available
or adequate as to a particular plaintiff, but on whether
‘Congress or the Executive has created a remedial process
that it finds sufficient to secure an adequate level of deterrence,’ as a prospective matter.”  Br.in.Opp.16 (quoting
Egbert, 596 U.S. at 498) (emphasis altered).  The Oversight
Act’s dependence on appropriations reinforces Congress’s
cautious, resource-conscious approach in this area.
Pet.Br.35 n.13.  That Congress provided “no damages
remedies,” Resp.Br.28, is precisely the point: It indicates
“Congress does not want a damages remedy,” and that
courts should not “superim pos[e]” one themselves.  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148-149; Egbert, 596 U.S. at 498.
4. Finding this context “new ” does not “effectively overrule Carlson.”  Resp.Br.29-32.  It respects the limits of
Carlson’s context under existing precedent.  For example,
recognizing a new context based on differences in immediacy or severity would not foreclose applying Carlson  in
cases that are damages or nothing, or where death results.

13

It may be that “the ARP and the PLRA” (and PATRIOT
and Oversight Acts) are now “implicated in every possible
claim that could arise under Carlson,” rendering Carlson
“moribund.”  Resp.Br.31; Gov’t.Br.23-25.  Acknowledging
that reality does not mean Carlson doesn’t apply “even on
its own facts.”  Resp.Br.32.  It means Carlson ’s “own
facts” no longer arise because of developments Carlson
did not (and largely could not) consider.  That is the natural consequence of the principl e that “special factors that
were not considered in previous Bivens cases”—including
“alternative remedies” and “legislative action”—render
succeeding contexts “new.”  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148.  Recognizing that has happened here is an application of precedent, not its overruling.
There are ample reasons to overrule Bivens and Carlson.  Pet.Br.40-48; pp. 16-23, infra.  But precedent dooms
Watanabe’s claim regardless.
C. Watanabe’s Invocation of the Westfall Act Is
Misplaced
Watanabe’s theory that the Westfall Act’s passage “in
1988” compels an expansive view of Carlson ’s “context,”
Resp.Br.17, is unfounded.  As  discussed below, pp. 19-21,
infra, the Westfall Act was not a “response to Carlson” or
Bivens, Resp.Br.16.  It responded to “Westfall v. Erwin,”
484 U.S. 292 (1988), which Co ngress characterized as
“seriously erod[ing] the common law tort immunity previously available to Federal employees.”  Pu b. L. No. 100-
694, 102 Stat. 4563, § 2(a)(3)-(5), (b) (1988) (emphasis
added).  The Westfall Act sought to restore the FTCA “as
the sole means for compensating persons injured by” federal employees’ “common law torts.”  Ibid.  Congress
deliberately avoided addressing Bivens  claims, to which
the Act “ ‘does not extend or apply.’ ”  § 5 (codified at 28
U.S.C. § 2679(b)(2)(A)).

14

Accordingly, this Court has held that the Westfall Act
“certainly does not suggest” that “Congress ‘intended for
a robust enforcement of Bivens remedies.’ ”  Hernández,
589 U.S. at 111 n.9.  It is “not a license to create a new
Bivens remedy in a [new] context,” or grounds for taking
a capacious view of prior Bivens contexts.  Ibid.  The Act
“simply left Bivens where it found it,” ibid.—in the hands
of this Court.
Watanabe’s theory thus fa ils on its own terms.  Carlson’s context was the same in 1988 as it is today: A case
where an inmate had died in emergent circumstances; it
was “damages or nothing”; and the Court did not consider
the ARP or succeeding legislation.  By 1988, moreover,
this Court had adopted its “cautiou[s]” approach “to suggestions that Bivens remedies be extended into new contexts.”  Schweiker v. Chilicky, 487 U.S. 412, 421 (1988).  It
had recognized the significance of “congressional unwillingness to provide * * * damages for unconstitutional
deprivations.”  Id. at 426.  It had emphasized the risk of
“disruption” from judicial “intrusion” into other branches’
operations.  United States v. Stanley, 483 U.S. 669, 682-
683 (1987).  And it had made clear that alternative remedial structures can bar a Bivens remedy even if they “ ‘do
not provide complete relief ’ ” or are “ ‘not as effective as an
individual damages remedy.’ ”  Egbert, 596 U.S. at 493, 498
(quoting Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, 372, 388 (1983); citing Schweiker, 487 U.S. at 425-426).  The Westfall Act did
not disturb those principles, which make this context new.
Watanabe cites pre-Westfall Act dicta describing Carlson as involving a claim “ ‘under the Eighth Amendment’s
proscription against cruel and unusual punishment.’ ”
Resp.Br.17 (quoting Stanley, 483 U.S. at 678; citing
Schweiker, 487 U.S. at 421).  He overlooks that Carlson
itself specified that the inmate “died” within “hours.”  446

15

U.S. at 16 & n.1.  And his theory proves too much.  If Carlson’s “context” were simply “ ‘cruel and unusual punishment’ ” claims, Resp.Br.17, then Malesko, Minneci, and
Goldey would be wrongly decided.  Under Watanabe’s
logic, Bivens’s context would encompass any “Fourth
Amendment violation by federal officers,” Schweiker, 487
U.S. at 421—contrary to Ziglar , Hernández, and Egbert.
This Court rejects framing the new-context inquiry at
such a high level of abstraction.  A “new Bivens context”
can arise even if the “right” and “mechanism of injury” are
“the same” as in prior cases.  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 139;
Pet.Br.30.  So, too, here.
D. Watanabe’s Bivens Claim Cannot Proceed
Watanabe concedes that, if his case presents a new context at Bivens step one, special factors foreclose his claim
at step two.  Pet.Br.39-40; see Resp.Br.33 (agreeing “Carlson * * * should not be extended”).  That concession also
cements that this case does present a new context.  The
two steps “often resolve to a single question: whether
there is any reason to think that Congress might be better
equipped to create a damages remedy.”  Egbert, 596 U.S.
at 492.  If special factors suffice to foreclose a Bivens claim
at step two, and were not considered in prior Bivens cases,
they necessarily are meaningful enough to present a new
context at step one.
That analysis does not “eliminate the first step entirely,” Resp.Br.31; it honors the integral connection between
the two steps.  It is Watanabe’s (and the Ninth Circuit’s)
blinkered approach to step one that does violence to the
established Bivens framework: It would allow Bivens
claims to proceed despite powerful reasons—never considered by this Court—indicating Congress is better suited to make the call.

16

II. BIVENS SHOULD BE OVERRULED
Since Bivens, the Judiciary has relinquished much of its
incursion into Congress’s power to create damages remedies.  But Bivens, Davis, and Carlson remain conspicuous
outposts on that terrain.  So long as they stand, they strain
the separation of powers and deter Congress from reclaiming and reforming the zone itself.  Rather than perpetuate
the empty—yet costly—false hope of Bivens and its progeny, this Court should return the issue to the legislative
branch once and for all.  Forty-five years spent reining in
Bivens’s mischief is more than enough.
Watanabe cannot defend Bivens and Carlson on the
merits, and his contention that the Westfall Act or PLRA
“ratified” them defies statutor y text, history, and precedent.  So Watanabe offers a Bivens compromise: “This far
and no further.”  Resp.Br.1, 33-34, 47.  But that cannot
salvage Watanabe’s clai m, which would take Carlson
“further.”  See pp. 3-15, supra.  And it does not resolve the
fundamental conflict dividing lower courts: What is “this
far” or “further”?  Despite the Court’s repeated efforts to
explain how “easily satisfied” the “new-context inquiry” is,
Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 149; see Hernández, 589 U.S. at 102;
Egbert, 596 U.S. at 491-492, that issue continues to generate “ ‘multiple deep circuit splits,’ ” Pet.Br.44-45.  Another
decision trying to confine Bivens, Davis, and Carlson  to
their “own context[s],” Resp.Br.33, is unlikely to foreclose
dispute over what those contexts are.  Nor does it cure the
basic separation-of-powers problem: Whatever contexts
those cases occupy, that territory—creating damages remedies—properly belongs to Congress.
A. The Court Has Repudiated Bivens and Its Progeny
This Court has repeatedly rejected Bivens ’s premises
as inconsistent with the separation of powers.  Because
creating damages remedies is a quintessentially legisla-

17

tive endeavor, this Court has sworn off creating damages
remedies itself.  And it has rejected the notion that a bare
grant of jurisdiction authoriz es federal courts to create
causes of action that Congre ss has not.  Pet.Br.40-44.
Watanabe denies none of that.
Watanabe protests that “this case is about Carlson, not
Bivens.”  Resp.Br.33.  But Carlson bears Bivens’s defects,
and then some.  The only authority Carlson cited for creating a damages remedy was Bivens.  446 U.S. at 18.
Carlson, moreover, justified a “Bivens remedy” based on
Congress’s failure to explicitly prohibit it and the perceived inadequacy of a remedy Congress did create, 446
U.S. at 19-23—rationales this  Court has since rejected,
Pet.Br.43-44.  Carlson even announced ipse dixit that Bivens allows “punitive damages” because the Court thought
that would provide a better “deterrent.”  446 U.S. at 21-22.
But this Court has rejected that, too, holding that “calibration” of “deterrence” “must be left to Congress, not the
federal courts.”  Egbert, 596 U.S. at 498.  Nothing remains
of Carlson’s (or Bivens’s, or Davis’s) foundation.  That this
Court had already “repudiated” inferring damages remedies under statutes when Carlson was decided, Resp.Br.43
n.3, shows that Carlson was out of step with precedent
from the outset.
Watanabe’s effort to analogize Carlson to common-law
actions against jailers and other officials, Resp.Br.40-42,
fails.  Carlson invoked no such history.  There is “no basis
for the Court to give preceden tial sway to reasoning that
it has never accepted” to salvage “a conclusion reached on
different grounds that have since been abandoned or
discredited.”  Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310, 384
(2010) (Roberts, C.J., concu rring).  And this Court has
already rejected “[a]nalogizing Bivens to the work of a
common-law court.”  Hernández, 589 U.S. at 100.  “With

18

the demise of federal general common law, a federal court’s
authority to recognize a damages remedy must rest at
bottom on a statute enacted by Congress.”  Id. at 101.
The “tradition” Watanabe invokes, Resp.Br.40, involved
state common-law claims against fede ral officials, where
the alleged unconstitutionality of their actions served to
defeat a defense of federal authorization.  Hernández, 589
U.S. at 110-111; Pet.Br.4-5, 44.  (Such suits are now channeled through the FTCA.)  Bivens and Carlson spurned
reliance on state-law damages claims in favor of a new
federal damages claim of the Court’s own making.  Bivens
v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents , 403 U.S. 388,
394-395 (1971); Carlson, 446 U.S. at 23-25; cf. Resp.Br.21
(Carlson contravened “traditional” common-law rule that
“ ‘no civil action lies for an injury which results in death’ ”).
Just 8 years before Bivens, this Court had refused to
create such a remedy.  Wheeldin v. Wheeler, 373 U.S. 647,
652 (1963); Pet.Br.44.  By inventing a federal damages
remedy for alleged cons titutional violations, Bivens and
Carlson did not follow tradition—they “broke” it.  Hernández, 589 U.S. at 99.
Watanabe urges that “uniquely federal interests” justify federal common-lawmaking in the “enclave” of “ ‘civil
liability of federal officials for actions taken in the course
of their duty.’ ”  Resp.Br.39 (quoting Boyle v. United Technologies Corp. , 487 U.S. 500, 505 (198 8)).  But federal
common law applies where “displ acement of state law” is
“necessary” to protect federal interests—such as by
limiting officials’ liability under state law.  Boyle, 487 U.S.
at 504-505.  Watanabe cites no instance where the Court
invoked federal common law to create a damages remedy
against federal officials.  Doing so is especially inappropriate in the “federal enclave” of running a “prison,”
Resp.Br.39, a matter “peculiarly within the province of the

19

legislative and executive branches,” Turner v. Safley, 482
U.S. 78, 84-85 (1987).
B. Nothing Justifies Retaining Bivens
Bivens, Davis, and Carlson lost their analytical foundation long ago.  Any practica l justification for their retention has evaporated, too.  They offer plaintiffs only “ ‘false
hope,’ ” yet inflict a heavy toll on targeted federal employees.  Pet.Br.47-48.  They ha ve also proved unworkable,
creating conflict after conflict.  Pet.Br.44-45.  While Watanabe insists this case will make applying Bivens “straightforward,” Resp.Br.46, the Court presumably had the same
aspiration in Ziglar, Hernández, Egbert, and Goldey.  But
lower-court confusion continues to require this Court’s
intervention.  Bivens will be straightforward only when it
is gone.
1. Reliance interests cannot save Bivens.  Pet.Br.45-
47.  Watanabe does not assert  reliance by “future plaintiffs.”  Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe, 609 U.S. 141, 154 (2026).
And his protest that overruling Carlson would leave federal prisoners “with no reme dy at all,” Resp.Br.45, is
incorrect.  Carlson-like injuries can be asserted as medical
negligence claims under the FT CA.  Pet.Br.46.  Likewise
with Bivens-like torts by law-enforcement agents.  Ibid.
Watanabe’s real complaint is that damages would run
against the deep-pocketed United States, not “against the
responsible officer.”  Resp.Br. 45.  But individual liability
is already unavailable for countless constitutional violations—including cruel-and-unusual “excessive force” by
“federal prison officials.”  Goldey, 606 U.S. at 943-944.
Non-damages remedies remain.  See pp. 8-12, supra.  And
Congress can create any other remedies it deems desirable.
2. Watanabe’s contention that Congress “relied on” and
“ratified” Carlson through the Westfall Act, Resp.Br.34,
37, 43-44, is fiction.  In Watanabe’s telling, the Westfall Act

20

“extinguished the traditional remedy of using state common law to hold individual fe deral officers liable in damages” “only on the understanding that the constitutional
claims recognized in Bivens and Carlson would remain
available.”  Resp.Br.34.  The Act’s text refutes that story.
It explains Congress’s understanding that federal employees had long been “ protected from personal common law
tort liability by a broad based immunity.”  102 Stat. 4563,
§ 2(a)(3) (emphasis added).  “For more than 40 years”—
since the FTCA’s 1946 enactm ent—“the Federal Tort
Claims Act ha[d] served as the sole means for compensating persons injured by” fede ral employees’ common-law
torts.  § 2(a)(1), (3).
Congress believed, however, that “Westfall v. Erwin”
had “seriously eroded the common law tort immunity
previously available to Federal employees” by limiting it
to discretionary acts.  § 2(a)(4) (emphasis added); see Westfall, 484 U.S. at 300.  The Westfa ll Act responded to that
“immediate crisis” by (in Congress’s view) restoring the
common-law-tort immunity federal employees had enjoyed
and reinstating the FTCA as the “ ‘exclusive’ ” remedy for
federal employees’ “common law torts.”  § 2(a)(3), (b); § 5
(codified at 28 U.S.C. § 2679(b)(1)).  The Westfall Act thus
did not “extinguis[h]” exis ting common-law remedies
against federal employees because (much less “only”
because) Bivens remained a backstop.  Resp.Br.34.  The
Act was a targeted effort to restore an immunity from
common-law-tort liability that predated Bivens—while
providing a damages remedy against the government.2

2 While Westfall viewed traditional common-law-tort immunity more
narrowly, 484 U.S. at 297-298 & n.4, what matters is that Congress
understood the Westfall Act as restoring preexisting immunity from
common-law-tort liability, not “tak[ing] away a preexisting right of
action,” Resp.Br.44.

21

Far from cementing Bivens in place, the Westfall Act
steered clear, declaring it “ ‘does not extend or apply to’ ”
constitutional claims.  102 Stat. 4564, § 5 (codified at 28
U.S.C. § 2679(b)(2)(A)).  The Act “simply left Bivens where
it found it”—in the hands of courts.  Hernández, 589 U.S.
at 111 n.9; see pp. 13-15, supra.
While Watanabe invokes generic legislative history,
Resp.Br.34, he overlooks on-p oint history demonstrating
Congress’s deliberate choice to take no position  on
Bivens.  As House sponsor Barney Frank explained, there
was “general agreement on a quick and easy reversal of
Westfall.”  Legislation to Amend the Federal Tort Claims
Act: Hearing Before Subcomm.  on Admin. Law & Gov’tl
Relations of H. Comm. on the Judiciary, 100th Cong. 194-
195 (1988).  But “constitutional  torts” presented “a separate and much more controvers ial issue” that could make
a “non-controversial vote” a  “more controversial” one.  Id.
at 40, 195.  Consequently, “a ll sides agree[d]” they “ d[id]
not want to do anything ” regarding Bivens that might
“impinge one way or the other in that controversy.”  Id. at
40 (emphasis added); see 134 Cong. Rec. 29,933 (1988)
(sponsor Sen. Grassley: “this bill does not have any effect
on the so-called Bivens case s”).  That’s why Congress
specified that the Act “ ‘does not extend or apply’ ” to constitutional claims.  102 Stat. 4564, § 5 (codified at 28 U.S.C.
§ 2679(b)(2)(A)).  That disclaimer cannot be rewritten into
an endorsement of Bivens.
Nor did the PLRA ratify Carlson.  Resp.Br.35.  While
the PLRA creates a “procedural framework” for such
claims, Resp.Br.36, that’s because it governs all prisoner
suits under “section 1983 * * * or any other Federal law,”
42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a); see pp. 10-11, supra.  That it “contemplates the existence of money damages,” Resp.Br.35,
is unremarkable given that § 1983 and other statutes auth-

22

orize damages.  The PLRA itself does not provide a damages remedy.  Goldey, 606 U.S. at 944.  That “suggest[s]
that Congress does not want a damages remedy”—the
opposite of ratifying Carlson.  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 148.
At most, the Westfall Act and PLRA show that Congress has not affirmatively eliminated Bivens and Carlson.  But this “Court has jettisoned many precedents that
Congress likewise could have  legislatively overruled”—
especially where, as here , those precedents involve
“judicial invention” beyond the Judiciary’s proper role.
Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 411
(2024).  Here, moreover, Congress confronted uncertainty
over whether it could eliminate Bivens.  Pet.Br.47 n.15.
While Watanabe properly agrees Congress can do so,
Resp.Br.38, Justice Scalia observed that “an ‘implication’
imagined in the Constitution can presumably not even be
repudiated by Congress,” Correctional Services Corp. v.
Malesko, 534 U.S. 61, 75 (2001) (S calia, J., concurring);
accord Minneci v. Pollard, 565 U.S. 118, 131 (2012) (Scalia, J., concurring).  Even today, Watanabe’s amicus insists
Congress cannot eliminate Bivens  without constitutional
“amendment.”  Cato.Br.4.
3. Because “judicially created  causes of action offend
the separation of powers in almost every circumstance,”
Cisco “close[d] the door” on judicially created Alien Tort
Statute liability.  609 U.S. at  153, 155.  For the same reason, the Court should close th e door on judicially created
Bivens liability.  Pet.Br.41-43.   Watanabe observes
(Resp.Br.33) that Cisco did not foreclose ATS suits for the
so-called “Blackstone three” torts recognized at common
law.  609 U.S. at 155.  But those torts are “not * * * evidence”
that federal “courts [have] authority to create causes of
action”—they predated the ATS and the Framing.  Id. at
155 n.3.  The “Bivens three” ha ve no such pedigree.  This

23

Court invented them starting in 1971, two centuries after
the Bill of Rights’ adoption in 1791.  Their legitimacy rests
entirely on federal courts’ power to create damages remedies—a power “mo[st] accurately described as nonexistent.”  Id. at 145.3
CONCLUSION
The judgment should be reversed.
